title: Section 8 Rent-Increase Deadline Capture Service
one_liner: A tracker that knows each voucher tenant's lease anniversary, sees the new FY2027 payment standard, and files the landlord's rent-increase request inside the tight 60-day window before a year of raise is forfeited.
customer: Small landlords with 1 to 50 Housing Choice Voucher units, especially out-of-state investors in Section 8-heavy markets such as Memphis, Cleveland, St. Louis and Indianapolis. Small PM firms with voucher portfolios are the second segment.
problem: Housing-authority payment standards rose for FY2027, but a new standard does not flow through to an existing tenancy on October 1. It applies only at each tenant's lease anniversary. The owner must send a written request within a typically tight window, often 60 days before that date, or forfeit the increase for a year. Each housing authority has its own forms and dates. Most small owners never map the anniversary dates, so they leave real money uncollected. One market analysis found 3-bedroom increases of 6 to 12%, with a median of 10%.
solution: The landlord uploads photos of their HAP contracts and leases, and the tool extracts tenant anniversary dates and current contract rents. The team maintains a database of housing-authority payment standards and each authority's request process (scraped from PHA PDFs and notices, human-verified). For each unit it computes the increase headroom, alerts at 90, 75 and 60 days before the window closes, and generates the authority-specific rent-increase request letter or form. It tracks proof of submission and logs who was contacted and when. It also flags likely mistakes in the original rent-reasonableness record (wrong bedroom count or square footage) that justify a correction request mid-lease.
why_now: FY2027 standards take effect around October 1, 2026, and today is 2026-09-28. Anniversary windows are opening across the country right now. The forum thread on this appeared within days, and the one-year forfeiture is a hard deadline that makes people spend money.
revenue_model: Success-aligned pricing: $5 per unit per month, plus 1 month of the captured increase for each unit where the request is approved. On a $1,300 rent and a 10% bump, that is $130 per month, or $1,560 a year, per unit. Authority data is the moat; a PM-firm plan can charge per door. Later, a similar deadline tracker can cover annual recertification and inspection dates.
non_obvious_insight: The money is lost to a calendar, not to the tenant or the market, and the people who feel it are the least likely to be organized. A BiggerPockets post titled 'Section 8 rents went up for FY2027. Most landlords won't collect it' says: 'A new payment standard does not flow through to an existing tenancy on October 1'. It adds that owners must submit written requests within a typically tight 60-day window before each anniversary or forfeit the opportunity for an entire year. It reports 3-bedroom rates up 6-12% (median 10%) in nine of ten low-cost ZIP codes, and notes that St. Louis adopted its FY2027 standards effective Jan 1, 2027 (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/52/topics/1301792-section-8-rents-went-up-for-fy2027-most-landlords-wont-collect-it). Out-of-state voucher landlords also struggle with local rules, as in a Cleveland thread on Section 8 inspection standards (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1302305-furnace-and-water-heater-on-wood-platforms-cleveland-section-8-inspection). A separate thread notes Section 8 tenants are 'already at maximum allowable rates' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1302138-how-realistic-is-it-to-raise-rents-100-on-existing-tenants).
first_30_days: Week 1: hand-build payment-standard tables and request procedures for 3 housing authorities (start with St. Louis, Cleveland and Memphis). Publish a free calculator, 'How much did you leave on the table this year?', in the BiggerPockets Out-of-State and Landlording forums. Weeks 2 to 3: onboard 15 landlords, send requests manually with the templates, and track approvals. Week 4: turn on success-fee billing, and pitch 3 small voucher-heavy PM firms. Target: 15 landlords, 100+ units, and 10 documented approved increases.

title: Fast-Pay Administrator for Funded Home Repair
one_liner: Run the paperwork and pay small contractors in days on grant- and program-funded repairs (weatherization, aging-in-place, municipal repair programs) where waitlists exist because few pros will bid.
customer: Nonprofits, community action agencies, Area Agencies on Aging, housing authorities and municipal home-repair programs with budgets but weak execution capacity.
problem: Programs have money but not throughput: jobs are small ($2-15K), paperwork-heavy (income verification, lead-safe rules, photos, inspections) and reimbursed in 30-90 days. Good contractors are too busy for low-margin, slow-pay work. The median home is 44 years old, repair-over-replace is at 62%, and homeowners cannot get quotes.
solution: Act as general contractor of record plus payment desk: take the program's approved scope, match it to vetted small pros, run documentation and inspections in a phone workflow, pay the pro in 5-7 days by fronting cash, and bill the agency with audit-ready files. The agency's program-delivery budget line pays the admin fee.
why_now: Aging housing stock and record remodeling spend ($524B) mean small pros have plenty of alternatives to slow-pay work. Vision and document models make photo-based compliance cheap. Slower remodeling growth (about 1.6% by year-end) should free some pro capacity for steady program work.
revenue_model: 12-18% admin fee on job value paid by the agency, plus a 1-2% factoring spread on advances.
non_obvious_insight: In public repair programs the scarce input is neither money nor eligible homeowners, it is good contractors' willingness to endure paperwork and slow pay. Fast payment plus document automation is the moat, and the customer already has a budget line for program delivery.
first_30_days: Approach five agencies with waitlists in one state. Offer a 10-job cost-plus pilot. Recruit 10 small pros on a 7-day-pay promise. Open a $75K working-capital line and run documentation through simple phone forms.

title: Proof-of-Hours for Medicaid Work Requirements
one_liner: A text-message-first evidence engine that helps gig, seasonal, cash and caregiving enrollees document the 80-hour requirement, paid by managed care plans and safety-net providers for each member retained.
customer: Medicaid managed care plans (revenue is capitation per member), FQHC networks, hospital systems and county health departments carrying uncompensated care. Not the states: federal law bars plans from determining compliance, but outreach and enrollee assistance are allowed.
problem: From 1 Jan 2027, expansion adults 19-64 must show 80 hours a month of work, study or service. CMS projects 2.3 million people lose coverage in FY2027, largely through paperwork failure rather than true non-compliance. Georgia Pathways enrolled only about 16,000 people against roughly 359,000 potentially eligible. Irregular earners (gig, day labor, home care, seasonal, informal) have no clean payroll record, and states mostly rely on payroll data that misses them.
solution: A multilingual SMS, WhatsApp and app 'hour ledger'. It pulls earnings from gig and payment platforms via consented bank or statement links, sends one-tap SMS attestations to employers and clients, and logs volunteer and caregiving hours via QR check-in at partner churches and food banks. It screens for exemptions (medical frailty, caregivers) and outputs the evidence pack in each state's format, with renewal reminders every six months. The member owns the data and the plan sees only consented status.
why_now: Nebraska began enforcement on 1 May 2026. CMS issued its interim final rule on 3 June 2026 defining verification and the 80-hour test, and states did outreach in mid-2026. The national start is 1 Jan 2027 with six-month renewals, and plans are amending contracts now.
revenue_model: A per-member retention bounty ($40-$120 per successful renewal) or PMPM of $2-$6 for high-risk members, paid by plans. FQHC and hospital subscriptions, and later state contracts for outreach.
non_obvious_insight: The fight is not over who is eligible but over who can prove it. Compliant-but-undocumented workers are a large share of those at risk. The party with the strongest incentive to close that gap is not the state but the plan or provider whose revenue disappears with each disenrolled member. Verified hours are a portable asset the member can reuse at every renewal.
first_30_days: Partner with one FQHC network in a live or early-start state such as Nebraska. Hand-run a pilot for 200 enrollees using SMS plus a form, and build evidence-pack templates that match the state portal. Pitch three regional plans on a no-upfront-cost, pay-per-member-retained deal. Get privacy and HIPAA review done before enrolling anyone.

title: Verified Colony-Strength Ledger for Commercial Beekeepers
one_liner: Third-party hive-strength verification and escrowed pollination contracts, turning bees into a gradeable, financeable commodity after record die-offs.
customer: Migratory commercial beekeepers running 1,000+ hives who truck colonies to California almonds and other crops. Almond and fruit growers are the counterparties.
problem: Surveys found commercial operations lost an average of about 62% of colonies between June 2024 and February 2025, and estimated the lost almond pollination income at more than $400M. Pollination is sold by phone brokers on 'frames of bees' standards that are verified by spot manual inspection, so disputes and 'strength laundering' are common. Growers can't be sure what they get, beekeepers can't prove what they have, and lenders and insurers can't underwrite either.
solution: An inspector network using thermal imaging and frame-count sampling to grade colony strength before loading, with results stored in a tamper-evident ledger tied to each yard and hive. Strength-tiered pollination contracts with escrowed payments released on verified counts. Later, hive collateral reports for ag lenders, and parametric or indemnity cover for winter losses.
why_now: The 2024-25 losses were the worst on record, and 2025-26 survey and industry reports show continuing stress. Almond growers are paying about $181 per colony (2023 figure) for strong hives and demand certainty. Thermal and camera-based frame counting is now cheap. Almond bloom in February 2027 is about five months away, so a working pilot can earn first revenue this winter.
revenue_model: $4-8 per hive inspected, paid by the beekeeper and often co-paid by growers. A 2-3% fee on escrowed contract value. Later: data fees from ag lenders and insurance commissions.
non_obvious_insight: A beekeeper's scarcest asset is now the healthy colony, and the trade runs on trust and handshake grading. A neutral, standardized 'strength certificate' does three things at once: it lets strong operators charge more, it lets growers verify what they bought, and it creates the collateral data that lets banks lend against bees. The verifier becomes the exchange.
first_30_days: Contact 5-10 mid-size migratory beekeepers and 2-3 pollination brokers now (before winter loading). Hire or contract 2-3 experienced bee inspectors, and pilot thermal frame counting on 2,000 hives. Offer growers a paid 'verified load' program for the January-February 2027 loading window. Publish a strength-grade standard and get 2 growers to commit to tiered pricing.

title: Audit-Grade Inventory Robots for Defense Property
one_liner: Drone and rover inventory counts that produce tamper-evident audit evidence, sold first to defense contractors who must physically inventory government-furnished property, then to Pentagon depots racing a clean-audit deadline.
customer: Property managers at small and mid-size defense contractors (machine shops, depot-level repair firms, integrators holding government property). Later, DoD depots and audit-readiness contractors that need count observation.
problem: DoD has never passed a full financial audit and has set a clean-opinion goal of about 2028 (verify), and inventory and materiel existence are among the biggest obstacles. Leaders admit they lack supply-chain data to support a '90-, 120-, 180-day fight'. Federal staff capacity is shrinking (OPM rating caps, contested reorganizations) and agencies keep buying capacity. Contractors holding government property (FAR 52.245-1) must keep records and do periodic physical inventories that DCMA property administrators review, and the work is manual and labor-heavy.
solution: Deploy indoor drones, rovers and wearable scanners to produce time-stamped, geotagged, hash-chained count evidence reconciled to property records. Output exception lists in the format auditors and property administrators expect. Use offline-first, air-gapped operation, since air-gap-native tooling (Defense Unicorns) cut authorization from 18 months to about 2 weeks. Begin in low-hazard bays and add ordnance-safe hardware later.
why_now: Warehouse inventory drones matured in commercial logistics but were never packaged for federal audit evidence. The Pentagon's comfort with small drones jumped through Drone Dominance, and audit-readiness spending is a live budget line. Federal staffing cuts push work to contractors.
revenue_model: Per verified location or per count event, priced below manual count crews, with annual recurring programs for contractors. Later, per-depot audit-evidence programs through subcontracts.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not logistics but the CFO and audit-readiness office, which has a statutory deadline and money, while logistics chiefs have no robot budget. Selling robots as 'audit evidence' unlocks the funding. Contractor-held government property is a commercial beachhead with a private budget.
first_30_days: Recruit two defense contractors with large government-property holdings and one small audit or property-compliance firm. Do a free count at one facility to define the evidence format. Then price a paid annual inventory at each and pursue a small DLA or Army innovation solicitation.

title: Show Safe: Compliance and Theft Registry
one_liner: An operating layer for card-show and fan-convention promoters that handles vendor tax permits, insurance certificates, secure check-in and a shared stolen-slab registry.
customer: Promoters of card shows, comic and anime cons (thousands across the US) and vendor associations.
problem: State rules put promoters on the hook for collecting tax on admissions and verifying vendor permits (RI, NY and TX guidance). Armed robberies and thefts of collectors and vendors spiked in 2026 (CNN, April 2026; $100k stolen from a Burbank card store; about $10k stolen at Anime NYC). Promoters run on spreadsheets and Facebook groups.
solution: Vendor onboarding with per-state permit and tax-ID verification and insurance certificate upload, table booking and payments, badge check-in and out logs, incident reporting, and a registry of stolen graded-card cert numbers and serials that vendors and stores can scan-check. Optional admissions-tax filing.
why_now: The 2026 theft wave and insurer scrutiny make promoters want safety and paperwork rigor. The registry's value grows with every show that joins.
revenue_model: $150-500 per show SaaS, ~1.5% on payments, registry API access for stores, and insurance referrals.
non_obvious_insight: Promoters are the choke point where thousands of vendors meet, so the stolen-goods network effect belongs to whoever sees vendor flow. Compliance is the reason to sign up, and the registry is the moat.
first_30_days: Sign 10 local promoters with a free first show. Seed the registry from public theft reports on social media. Charge from show two.

title: Program Survival Analytics for Regional Universities
one_liner: A subscription that tells provosts which degree programs will fail the new federal earnings tests and loan-cap economics as AI hollows out their feeder occupations, with a redesign playbook.
customer: Provosts, institutional research offices and deans at regional universities, master's-heavy colleges and online providers ($20-60k a year), plus state systems.
problem: As I understand the 2025 budget law (verify specifics), programs whose graduates don't out-earn benchmarks can lose loan eligibility, and Grad PLUS ended for new borrowers with new caps from July 2026. Graduate programs in cognitive fields (analytics, MBA, MS CS, communications) rely on borrowing, while entry-level demand is falling (NY Fed: 42% recent-grad underemployment). Institutions see it only when enrollment drops.
solution: A program-level model combining College Scorecard earnings, occupation-level job-posting trends, AI-exposure scores and enrollment and borrowing data. It delivers early-warning flags, a scenario tool, recommended pivots (in-degree apprenticeships, short credentials, employer co-design) backed by real employer demand signals, and board-ready compliance reporting.
why_now: The new loan and accountability rules began July 2026, the AI-driven junior hiring freeze is measurable (Stanford: 19% gap for ages 22-25), and university budgets are tight.
revenue_model: Annual licence of $20-60k, program-redesign consulting and state-system contracts.
non_obvious_insight: Universities already face compliance deadlines, but nobody has tied AI exposure to the earnings-test math. A federal deadline creates budget urgency that 'future of work' advice never gets. The first programs to fail are likely master's degrees in cognitive fields.
first_30_days: Build the model from public Scorecard data for ~200 institutions as a proof. Generate 'programs at risk' reports for 20 target universities' master's programs and email institutional-research directors and provosts. Sell three $7.5k pilot diagnostics.

title: Water Towers as Virtual Power Plants
one_liner: Aggregate municipal pump stations and elevated tanks into a controllable flexible load that dodges peak-coincident charges and earns demand-response and capacity payments, with a hard guarantee on pressure and fire reserve and an operator veto.
customer: Cities and districts that pump water, especially cities that own both the electric and water departments (common in the Midwest, Texas and the Southeast) and utilities with transmission-level or large demand-charge accounts. The buyer is the utilities director or the city manager, with the finance director as the champion.
problem: Electricity is one of the largest controllable costs for a pumped water system. Yet most pumping schedules are simple level setpoints written years ago, and operators keep tanks fat out of habit and fear. The unspoken rule is that nobody ever got fired for a full tank. Meanwhile the grid has turned pumping hours into money. Peak-coincident charges such as 4CP in ERCOT and peak load contribution tags in PJM are set by just a handful of hours per year. Capacity prices have spiked in recent auctions. Big load additions are pushing retail rates up. Water utilities are physically able to shift a large share of pumping, but no vendor is selling it to the 10-100k-population systems in a form an operator trusts.
solution: A small edge box or cloud service that reads tank levels, pump status and pressure from SCADA (OPC-UA or Modbus, read-only at first). It computes safe curtailment windows per station with hard constraints: fire and emergency reserve never touched, minimum pressure kept, projected demand over the event covered, water-age limits respected. It pre-cools tanks before predicted grid peaks and auto-releases if any constraint is threatened. Operators see one screen and can veto or end an event in one tap. Phase one is pure peak-coincident avoidance and time-of-use shifting, which needs no market enrollment. Phase two enrolls the stations as a curtailment resource through a demand-response aggregator partner or directly.
why_now: Recent PJM capacity auctions cleared at or near the price cap, on the order of $100k or more per curtailable megawatt per year before an aggregator's cut. Data center load growth is pushing capacity and transmission costs into retail rates, and RTOs and utilities are expanding demand-response programs. Edge controllers and OPC-UA gateways are cheap, and small teams can now build reliable forecasting for tank levels and peak intervals. (Auction figures are from memory. Verify current prices before pitching.)
revenue_model: 25-40% of verified savings and demand-response revenue, with no upfront cost to the utility and a small monthly platform fee. Utilities with both electric and water departments can be sold a bundled controls contract.
non_obvious_insight: The constraint is not physical but psychological and legal: operators are (rightly) terrified of a pressure or fire-flow failure. The winning product is not optimization software but a guarantee with a veto. Sell the operator the ability to stop it at any moment and the CFO the savings. Also, water and electric are often the same city, and the city has never put both budgets on one page.
first_30_days: Target three small cities that own both electric and water in ERCOT or PJM territory and have published tariffs. Get read-only SCADA access at one pump station, or historical CSV exports of tank levels and pump runs. Replay a year of the data to show what a 4CP or PLC avoidance schedule would have saved with reserves untouched. Bring that dollar figure to the city manager, and sign a shared-savings pilot on one pump station.

title: Privacy-Compliant Monetization for Faith Apps
one_liner: An audit-plus-replacement stack for small prayer, Quran, Bible, Torah and temple apps whose ad SDKs quietly turn every user into a sale of religious-belief data.
customer: Independent and mid-size publishers of ad-funded faith apps (prayer times, Quran, Bible/devotional, Hindu calendar, Zmanim, halal finders, congregation apps) and church-management/giving software vendors serving thousands of congregations.
problem: Religious beliefs are special-category data under GDPR Art. 9 and 'sensitive data' requiring opt-in consent under nearly every US state privacy law. Maryland's law goes further, banning the sale of sensitive data and limiting collection to what is strictly necessary (in force since Oct 2025, verify enforcement dates). Regulators have treated mere use of a niche app as revealing sensitive traits (Norway's Grindr fine, upheld on appeal, verify). Reporting in 2020 showed a Muslim prayer app's location data reaching a broker and then US military contractors. Yet most small faith apps run stock ad SDKs with device IDs and location, have no consent flow and no counsel. The briefing notes non-Christian faith apps are far less served than Hallow-style Christian ones, and the IAPP says state privacy momentum is at an all-time high.
solution: (1) A public audit tool that scans app binaries and web properties for SDK data flows and issues a scorecard plus a legal-risk memo by state and EU. (2) A drop-in compliance SDK: a consent manager that treats every user as sensitive by default, server-side region logic, data maps and DPIA templates in Arabic, Urdu, Bahasa, Hebrew, Spanish and Portuguese. (3) A contextual, ID-free sponsorship marketplace where halal, kosher, umrah, church-goods and faith-nonprofit sponsors book placements by content context (for example an iftar-times page). (4) A subpoena and data-request playbook with minimal retention by design, so the app has little to hand over.
why_now: State privacy laws with sensitive-data opt-in are now the norm and Maryland's strict rules are enforceable in 2026 (verify dates). GDPR fines total EUR 7.16B with 229 new cases in 2026 (per briefing). Faith apps are booming (Hallow reached #1 in the US App Store) while faith data is politically charged around surveillance and immigration enforcement.
revenue_model: $149-499/month per app for SDK plus audit. 25-30% revenue share on contextual sponsorship. One-time $1.5-3k audit and fix sprint. Enterprise contracts with church-tech vendors.
non_obvious_insight: For a faith app the category itself reveals the belief (the Grindr logic), so 'we do not collect religion' is not a defense. The violation is the ad model, so the fix is a different revenue stream, not a policy PDF. Contextual sponsorship from faith-community advertisers can pay better than junk programmatic. Public scorecards create the sales funnel, because in tight communities reputation and fear move fast.
first_30_days: Audit the top 100 Muslim prayer/Quran apps and 50 Christian, Jewish and Hindu apps with open-source traffic analysis (mitmproxy, Exodus-style trackers). Publish a 'Privacy Scorecard for Faith Apps' and email each publisher. Sell paid fix sprints to 5 pilot apps at about $2k and recruit 5 community sponsors for contextual placements. Team is one privacy lawyer plus one Android engineer.

title: Designer Proteins for Clear Protein Water
one_liner: AI-designed acid-stable proteins that stay clear at pH 2.8-3.5, replacing whey in clear protein drinks.
customer: RTD beverage and sports-nutrition brands making clear protein waters.
problem: Whey uniquely gives clear drinks at pH 2.8-3.5, and no alternative matches it, so brands cannot swap out scarce whey.
solution: Computationally design candidate proteins for acid solubility and clarity, express them through a contract fermentation partner, and deliver a first clear-drink ingredient.
why_now: Protein-design models and cheap gene synthesis matured in 2025-26, and Verley's FDA-cleared fermentation whey shows the regulatory path for fermentation-derived proteins.
revenue_model: Development fees of $50-150k per brand, then per-kg supply or licensing.
non_obvious_insight: Alt-protein failed by trying to replicate all of dairy. The real gap is a single functionality in a single premium beverage format.
first_30_days: Design about 20 candidates, test solubility and turbidity at pH 3 with cell-free expression, and pitch 10 clear-protein brands for paid development.

title: Make Platforms and Receiving Banks Pay Scam Refunds
one_liner: A contingency-fee desk that packages evidence so banks can recover mandatory scam reimbursements from receiving institutions and, in the EU, from the platforms where the scam ran.
customer: UK and EU challenger banks, building societies, credit unions, and e-money and payment institutions. Buyers are fraud-recovery and operations heads.
problem: In the UK, PSPs have had to reimburse authorized push-payment scam victims up to GBP 85K since Oct 2024, with the cost split 50:50 between sending and receiving firms. The EU's provisional PSR deal extends liability to bank-impersonation scams and to platforms that ignore fraud notices. Banks treat reimbursement as a cost of business. Recovering from the other side of the chain (the mule-hosting bank, the ad or profile platform) is manual, slow, and mostly abandoned.
solution: Ingest reimbursed case files and auto-build claim dossiers: a timeline, hash-stamped screenshots of the scam ad or profile, the platform notification and its response time, mule-account indicators, and a funds trace. File claims through scheme channels and formal notices to platforms. Track deadlines and disputes. Get paid a percentage of what is actually recovered.
why_now: Mandatory reimbursement now has more than a year of claim volume in the UK. The EU deal shifts costs toward platforms. Investigations into scam-ad revenue have made platform accountability a political priority. Nobody yet holds the data on which counterparties pay and how fast.
revenue_model: 15-25% contingency on recovered value, with a small SaaS floor. A mid-size UK institution reimbursing GBP 10-30M a year can justify six-figure annual fees.
non_obvious_insight: Liability rules create a claims market. The value chain of counterparties is unbilled because banks were told to reimburse victims, not to chase others, and the recovery data is a compounding moat. Whoever holds it can also sell it to regulators.
first_30_days: Offer 10 UK EMIs and small banks a free audit of 50 reimbursed cases showing recoverable amounts from receiving-side firms and disputed shares. Sign contingency contracts with the first 3. Hire one ex-fraud-ops analyst and use spreadsheets and templates before automating.

title: One Guide, Twelve Languages: Live-Dubbed Tours
one_liner: The guide speaks once and each guest hears their own language in low-latency synthesised audio, so mixed-language groups share one guide and cities see fewer, fuller groups.
customer: Independent guides, small tour operators and shore-excursion companies in cities that cap groups (Venice, Rome, Florence, Amsterdam, Kyoto), plus guide associations and municipalities.
problem: Language-siloed tours multiply the number of groups on the same street, and group-size caps and guide quotas bind. Guides cannot fill rare-language tours, and whisper systems only amplify the guide's voice.
solution: Guide microphone to live speech translation to each guest's phone, joined by QR with no app install, with per-listener language choice, a glossary of place names, an offline fallback, headcount tools and translated questions back to the guide. Sell a clip mic and hub kit plus per-tour credits.
why_now: Real-time speech-to-speech translation became good enough in 2025 (consumer earbuds now offer live translation and APIs offer realtime speech), eSIM and 5G make connectivity easy, and cities are tightening group caps.
revenue_model: USD 39-99 per guide per month or USD 1-2 per guest, USD 150 kits and municipal licences.
non_obvious_insight: Language silos are a hidden multiplier of overtourism. Merging groups cuts the number of groups without cutting visitors, so guides earn more and cities become allies and customers.
first_30_days: Recruit 20 guides in Rome and Florence, pilot two-language tours then four, and measure latency and guest satisfaction. Approach the guide association with the pilot results.

title: Transformer Buying Co-op for Small Utilities
one_liner: Pool the orders of hundreds of rural co-ops and municipal utilities into one standardized spec so they can get in line together.
customer: Roughly 900 electric distribution co-ops and 2,000 municipal utilities, plus solar and storage developers. They pay a procurement fee.
problem: Power transformer lead times average 128 weeks, distribution transformer prices are up as much as 95%, and over 40M units are past service life. Small utilities order in dozens with bespoke specs and go to the back of the line. One contrarian says standardized units can ship in 12-14 months, so procurement, not manufacturing, is the bottleneck.
solution: Pre-negotiated framework agreements with two or three manufacturers (including offshore) for a small menu of standard units, for example pad-mount 25-167 kVA and 5-10 MVA substation units. Add a predictive replacement list built from age and AMI loading data, a financed rotating stock pool, and slot reassignment among members.
why_now: Data centers outbid utilities for manufacturing slots, lead times are at 128 weeks, and co-ops and munis are scrambling with no purchasing leverage.
revenue_model: 2-4% procurement fee, a stock-pool financing and storage spread, and $10-30k a year SaaS for replacement planning.
non_obvious_insight: Part of the shortage is fragmentation. Manufacturers prioritize buyers who commit to standard specs and volume, and small utilities are collectively huge but individually invisible.
first_30_days: Collect 30 co-op and muni transformer spec sheets. Propose a common spec at a state co-op association or APPA event. Get five utilities to sign LOIs for a 200-unit pilot order. Talk to two mid-size manufacturers with open 2028 slots.

title: Silver Crews: Retiree Work Co-ops for US Towns
one_liner: A membership co-op for retirees 62+ that contracts with towns, school districts and HOAs for short, insured, daytime jobs (crossing guards, school and library aides, grounds work, event staffing) and acts as employer of record.
customer: Municipal public-works and parks departments, school districts, libraries, HOAs and property managers who pay per job-hour. Retirees join as members.
problem: Employers with 5-15 hour-a-week daytime needs can't hire for them. Retirees want flexible, meaningful part-time work but distrust app gigs and can't easily get liability and accident cover. A record 4.18M Americans turned 65 in 2025, crossing guards are already the most senior-dominated occupation (nearly 1 in 3 are 65+), and about 15% of retirees say they'd consider returning to paid work.
solution: A county-level 'Silver Crew' modeled on Japan's Silver Human Resource Centers (about 1,300 centers, 700,000+ members). It recruits, background-checks and trains 200-400 members, holds standing contracts, schedules shifts, runs payroll (W-2 or contract), carries pooled workers'-comp/accident insurance, and hosts a monthly social meetup. Customers get a reliable pool without hiring headaches, and members get a community as well as a paycheck.
why_now: Peak 65 will stay elevated through at least 2027, school and municipal labor shortages persist, and municipal budgets favor contracting over adding headcount. Japan's centers have proven the model over decades, while US equivalents are small nonprofit senior-employment programs, not service-contract businesses.
revenue_model: Mark-up of roughly 15-25% on member pay billed to customers, small annual member dues, and margin on pooled insurance.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input isn't retiree labor, it's the wrapper. A town can't onboard a 68-year-old for six hours a week, but a co-op with pooled accident cover, one background-check process and a single invoice can. Japanese centers work because the arrangement is legally a contract for a task, not a job, which strips out friction. The social meetup is the retention engine, and it is what makes seniors choose this over Uber or DoorDash.
first_30_days: Pick one retiree-dense county (Florida, Arizona or a New England town). Sign 3 pilot contracts (an HOA, a school district and a library) using an existing PEO for payroll and workers' comp. Recruit 40 retirees through senior centers, churches and Nextdoor. Run the first paid shifts within 4 weeks and invoice monthly.

title: Cloud Machine Shop for High-School Shop Class
one_liner: Students design parts, watch real CNC machines cut them live at a partner job shop, and receive the parts by mail, so any school gets a hands-on manufacturing lab without machines or instructors.
customer: High-school and community-college CTE and robotics programs (per-project fees, often funded by CTE grants); job shops sponsor for recruiting.
problem: Manufacturing has openings, but CNC labs cost $100k+ and need instructors who are scarce, so rural and small schools cannot offer them. AI can now generate designs but students never touch real machining. Hands-on work is also the AI-resilient part of learning.
solution: A web portal: design in browser CAD with AI assist, automatic manufacturability checks and CAM by the partner shop, a scheduled live-stream slot where the machine cuts the student's part with a shop mentor narrating, then shipment. Curriculum aligns to entry-level machining credential levels and gives teachers a dashboard.
why_now: Text-to-CAD and instant-quote manufacturing platforms are good enough in 2026, streaming is trivial, and job shops have idle off-peak capacity and hiring pain. School AI pauses and screen fatigue make hands-on offerings attractive.
revenue_model: $25-60 per student project, $3-6k per classroom per year, plus recruiting sponsorship from job shops and manufacturer associations.
non_obvious_insight: Equipment and instructors are the constraint, not student interest. Machines already run from files, so the lab can be teleported, and idle night-shift capacity is a free asset that the shop's hiring pain will pay to use.
first_30_days: Partner with one local job shop with a couple of machines available off-peak. Recruit 5 CTE or robotics teachers. Run a 3-week design-and-cut unit at $30 per student and measure engagement. Map the unit to a machining credential standard.

title: Shoot-Out Co-Own: Legal OS for Friend Homebuyers
one_liner: A co-ownership package for friend groups: a state-specific ownership agreement with a built-in Texas-shoot-out buyout, contribution-weighted equity, default rules and lender-friendly structure.
customer: Groups of 2-4 unrelated Gen Z and younger-millennial earners (friend pods, siblings, single buyers) in high-cost metros, referred by buyers' agents, mortgage brokers and credit unions.
problem: Surveys show roughly a third of Gen Z considering co-buying and about 60% of renters open to it, yet actual co-buying is rare because it is legally scary. What if someone wants out, marries, loses a job or dies? Lenders and title companies improvise, and disputes end friendships. First-time buyers now reach ownership around age 40, so the pressure to pool is real.
solution: A standardized co-ownership stack: a state-specific tenancy-in-common or LLC agreement, a scheduled shoot-out exit (one owner names a price, the others must buy or sell at it, which forces a fair price without appraisals or lawsuits), rights of first refusal, contribution-weighted equity with cure-period and dilution remedies for missed payments, and a shared sinking fund. It includes a multi-borrower mortgage broker network and a ledger that tracks each owner's cash and sweat equity. Life-event amendments handle marriage, job loss and death.
why_now: Co-buying interest is at record highs in 2026 surveys (Bank of America found about 32% of Gen Z considering it, and Rocket found about 60% of renters considering it), while median first-time buyer age hit a record near 40 in 2025. Lenders are courting co-borrowers and there is no dominant standard exit document.
revenue_model: $1,500-$3,000 per group for the legal package, $15 per month for the ledger and reminders, $1,000-$2,500 referral fees per funded loan, title and insurance affiliate fees, and a 1% fee to administer a shoot-out at exit.
non_obvious_insight: The friction is not wanting to co-buy, it is the exit. A shoot-out clause borrowed from partnership law gives every co-owner a fair way out and doubles as price discovery. Whoever owns the standard exit template becomes the SAFE-note of co-ownership.
first_30_days: Partner with five buyers' agents and two mortgage brokers in high-cost metros such as Seattle, Denver, Boston and the Bay Area. Recruit friend groups from first-time-buyer and house-hacking communities. Have a real-estate attorney draft templates for two states. Sell 10 pilot packages at $1,500, refunded if the deal does not close.

title: Compute-Heated Housing: GPUs as the Boiler Room
one_liner: Put a liquid-cooled AI rack in an apartment tower's mechanical room and use its waste heat as the building's hot-water plant, cutting utility costs while hosting power-starved compute.
customer: Owners of 200-500 unit towers or planned conversions with central hot-water plants, especially in cities with building-emissions caps, paired with inference and neocloud operators seeking power and cooling.
problem: 20.7% of renters cannot pay utilities in full, gas boilers face per-ton fines under building-performance laws (NYC Local Law 97 tightens in 2030), and AI compute is starved for sites with power and cooling.
solution: Install one direct-liquid-cooled rack (about 100-130 kW) in the mechanical room. Capture waste heat, lift it with heat pumps to domestic hot water, and sell the building heat at a discount to gas or provide it free in exchange for hosting. The compute operator pays colocation rent, and we own design, integration and the thermal contract. Later expand to space heating and whole conversions.
why_now: Dense liquid-cooled racks produce capturable heat, AI power scarcity is acute, heat-pump hot water is mature, and building-emissions caps are tightening.
revenue_model: Heat-as-a-service at 30-40% of avoided energy cost, hosting margin share, and $25-50K design fees per building.
non_obvious_insight: By rough engineering estimate, a 300-unit building's average hot-water load (about 100-120 kW thermal) roughly equals one AI rack's heat output. The boiler room can host compute that cannot be sited elsewhere, and hot-water demand never sleeps. Precedents exist in Europe (data-furnace heaters and pool heating).
first_30_days: Run feasibility on five NYC and Chicago buildings with emissions-cap exposure. Get a letter of intent from one inference host for a 100 kW pilot. Sell three paid feasibility studies at $10-15K and line up host-funded pilot capex.

title: Legal Price Bargaining Co-ops for Salmon Fleets
one_liner: Back-office software and staff that let independent salmon boats negotiate price as one bloc under the 1934 Fishermen's Collective Marketing Act, as the Bering Sea crab fleet already does.
customer: Member-owned fishermen's associations, starting with one district of 150-400 permit holders that sells to only 1-3 buyers (a Kodiak, Chignik, Cook Inlet, Prince William Sound or Southeast group, not Bristol Bay first). The association pays us. Its dues are collected as a small settlement deduction, about 0.25-0.5% of landed value.
problem: A salmon fisherman is a price-taker. The processor posts a base price and a bonus schedule in June, the boat delivers before it knows the final price, and the retros show up months later. Bristol Bay's average ex-vessel price went from $1.03 in 2025 to $1.72 in 2026, and 2026's $260M fishery came off only 30.1M fish. Nobody on the fishing side of that swing had a seat at the table. Meanwhile most skippers believe acting together is illegal price fixing, so the bar talk about a tie-up dies every spring.
solution: A compliance-first toolkit for member-owned associations. It includes counsel-reviewed charter and bylaw templates under 15 U.S.C. 521-22 and CFEC permit verification at sign-up. Members can vote by SMS. A firewalled clean team collects member-submitted price, volume and quality data. From that it builds a formula price tied to public benchmarks (wholesale frozen sockeye quotes, roe prices, yen and euro, canned prices) plus a quality bonus schedule. We supply the negotiators, contract templates (multi-year formula price, settlement deadlines, audit rights) and dues collection through settlement deductions. The association is the bargaining party and we are the vendor, so we never bargain or set prices ourselves.
why_now: The 2025 crash and 2026 rebound showed the fleet how much money moves on one posted number. Processors now compete with loyalty and quality bonuses (for example $0.15 for RSW, $0.05 bleeding, $0.05 chilling). Bonuses are a formula, and formulas can be negotiated. Cheap e-sign, SMS voting and LLM contract review make an association nearly free to run. The crab fleet's Alaska Marketing Association proves the model works in Alaska.
revenue_model: $2-5K/month retainer per association, or 10-15% of dues. On a $260M fishery, 0.25% dues is about $650K/year, so a full-district association is a $65-100K/year account. Later add multi-association benchmarking subscriptions and negotiation-support fees tied to price gains.
non_obvious_insight: The FCMA has let fishermen, not processors, bargain collectively since 1934. The fear that bargaining equals price fixing comes from the DOJ case where processors were the defendants (Pan Alaska Fisheries). Associations fail on operations, not law: no clean data, no dues collection, no fast votes, no credible fallback. Outsiders assume the fleet lacks leverage, but what it lacks is a secretary's office with software.
first_30_days: Pay an antitrust and fisheries lawyer $10-15K for a 10-page FCMA playbook. Pick one small port with a near-monopsony buyer and hold 10 harbor and Facebook-group sessions. Get 30-50 permit holders to sign a non-binding letter of intent. Run a members-only survey of what each boat was actually paid, timed for settlement season (Oct-Dec). Publish a 'your fleet vs. the benchmark' report. Aim for one association signed at a $2K/month retainer by February, before prices post in late spring.

title: Vendor Exit Desk for Fleets and Contractors
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that gets small fleets and home-service contractors out of predatory software and telematics contracts, and recovers the money the vendors keep billing.
customer: Owner-operators and fleets of 5-200 trucks locked into telematics or ELD contracts (Samsara, Motive). Also HVAC, plumbing and electrical contractors on ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro or Jobber, and small property managers on AppFolio. The owner or office manager pays, and only out of money recovered or saved.
problem: These vendors sell month-to-month or 1-year terms, then enforce hidden multi-year renewals, exit fees, ship-date billing and auto-renew windows. Support is now AI-only, so the customer cannot reach a human who can fix it. One Samsara reviewer was charged $29,000 for a 3-year contract after negotiating 1 year. Another lost about $32,000 paying for unused devices for 1 year and 9 months. ServiceTitan customers report quoted exit fees of $22,000, $29,000 and $37,000. An AppFolio reviewer was billed a $1,290 cancellation fee and said cancelling took 4 months.
solution: The customer forwards the contract and 3 recent invoices. The service does six things. (1) Extract renewal dates and notice windows, then send certified-mail non-renewal notices on the right day. (2) Audit billing against reality: billing that started at ship date rather than install date, decommissioned trucks still billed, duplicate accounts, and charges after cancellation. (3) Build a dispute packet with the sales promises, the timeline, and a card-network chargeback filing where the payment was on a business card. (4) Negotiate with the vendor's retention or legal team, with a partner attorney handling demand letters so the desk does not practice law itself. (5) Handle the data export. (6) Refer the customer to a replacement vendor that pays a bounty for the switch.
why_now: The 1-2 star reviews are dated 2026. They show vendors under public-market pressure enforcing renewals and paywalling features, for example Samsara charging $10 per truck for a feature shown in the demo. They also show support moving to AI. A Housecall Pro review dated Sept 28, 2026 says 'No support unless you want to speak with AI', and a Tithe.ly reviewer says the same in Feb 2026. Customers have nobody to call, so a human escalation path is now something they will pay for.
revenue_model: 25-30% of recovered or avoided dollars, with no fee if nothing is recovered. A $199 flat billing audit for small accounts. A $300-$1,000 referral bounty from the competing vendor that wins each switched fleet or contractor. An optional $29 per vendor per year renewal-watch subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The leads identify themselves. Each reviewer posts the vendor, the dollar amount, the date and the grievance publicly, so the whole first-year pipeline is already listed. Evidence: Samsara ($29,000 3-year contract, $32,000 unused devices, $900/month billed from ship date, $10/truck feature paywall) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/samsara.com. ServiceTitan ($22K, $29K and $37K exit quotes) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/servicetitan.com. Motive (renewal-window traps, charged again after cancelling) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/gomotive.com. AppFolio ($1,290 fee, 4-month cancellation) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/appfolio.com. Housecall Pro (charged $189 three times after cancelling, price doubled from $351 to $681) at https://www.trustpilot.com/review/housecallpro.com. The winning product is not software. It is a library of each vendor's contract clauses, notice windows and escalation paths, built up case by case, and it gets more effective with every dispute settled.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: pull the roughly 300 public 1-2 star reviews from the last 12 months across those 5 vendors and tag each by vendor, dollar amount and whether the customer is still active. Days 8-14: contact reviewers by the review reply or an email lookup, offering a free contract read. Sign a contract attorney on a small retainer. Days 15-30: take 5-10 contingency cases and publish 'how to cancel [vendor]' pages, since people search that phrase. Use the settled cases to build the clause library. Also pitch 2 competing telematics vendors on the switch bounty.

title: Corridor-Pivot Recruiting for Displaced Gulf Migrants
one_liner: When Gulf jobs disappear, retrain returnees and place them in Japan, Taiwan and Germany with the employer paying the fee.
customer: Employers in care, construction and manufacturing in East Asia and Europe that pay placement fees; the workers pay nothing.
problem: About $50bn of Gulf remittances is at risk. Returnees in Kerala, Nepal, Bangladesh and the Philippines carry recruitment debts and Gulf-specific credentials, and predatory agents will push them into worse corridors.
solution: A skills-credential wallet, language bootcamp and employer-paid placement pipeline, operated through a licensed recruitment partner. The wedge is care workers and welders from Kerala and Nepal for one Japanese or German employer.
why_now: The 2026 Iran-war energy shock displaced workers, and ageing economies are widening visa routes for care and trades.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k employer placement fee per worker, plus employer-paid training subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Displaced migrants are a supply shock nobody is organising. Employer-pays recruitment is both ethical and the direction of ILO fair-recruitment rules.
first_30_days: Sign one Kerala training institute and one overseas care-home operator, and run 30 candidates through a pilot.

title: Genki Tap: Konbini Clerks as Paid Elder Watchers
one_liner: Pay convenience-store staff to log a three-second 'seen and how they seemed' note on enrolled elderly regulars, and alert family and local support centers when someone goes quiet or drifts.
customer: Adult children living outside Osaka with a widowed or single parent in the city, at about ¥1,480 a month. Later customers are municipal community support centers (chiiki hokatsu shien centers) paying per enrolled senior, and eventually banks, trust banks and insurers that need early cognitive-decline and fraud signals.
problem: In 2025, 76,941 people died alone at home in Japan, 58,919 of them aged 65 or older. The Cabinet Office estimates about 22,222 were found after 8 or more days. Municipalities have signed 'elder-watching network' MOUs with konbini, post offices and newspaper carriers, but they are unpaid goodwill. The clerk notices, if that clerk happens to be on shift and cares, and the observation never becomes structured data. Owners know who has not come in for three days. We notice the customer buying the same item twice in a day, paying slowly with coins, forgetting the wallet, or getting confused at self-checkout. None of it reaches the family or the ward.
solution: The senior gets a keychain NFC tag or simply says a name. At the register, staff tap a ¥1,500 reader or a tablet and press one of three buttons: fine, a bit off, worried. If an enrolled senior is not seen for 48-72 hours, the system messages the family and a designated neighbor, then the local support center. The family gets a weekly digest such as 'came Mon, Wed, Thu; usual purchases; once forgot wallet'. The store earns ¥300-500 per enrolled senior per month, so the attention is paid for and survives shift changes. Consent is opt-in, data is minimal, and the escalation path runs through licensed care managers.
why_now: The National Police Agency now publishes annual solitary-death counts, and the 2025 figures show no decline. Municipalities are legally responsible for loneliness and isolation measures under the 2024 loneliness law. Post-2024 summer heat deaths at home have raised demand from families. Cashless and prepaid-card fraud aimed at seniors is also rising, so a clerk who already knows the customer is the best front-line filter.
revenue_model: Family subscription of ¥1,480 a month, of which ¥300-500 goes to the store. Municipal or support-center contracts pay per enrolled senior. Later, anonymized cognitive-drift signals feed paid programs from banks, trust companies and insurers concerned about dementia-related frozen assets and fraud.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource in elder monitoring is not sensors or AI, it is a trusted human who sees the person daily and is already 24/7 in the neighborhood. Municipal networks fail because the clerk's attention is unpaid and unstructured. A ¥300 payment plus a three-button interface turns free goodwill into reliable, recurring, auditable data. The store that sees the drift first is the konbini, not the clinic.
first_30_days: Enroll 8-10 owners in Ikuno, Nishinari, Higashinari and Abeno wards, starting with my own three stores. Use a LINE OA for families and cheap NFC readers or a phone app for staff. Identify 30 regulars whose adult children live in Tokyo, Nagoya or Fukuoka and pitch them by phone; aim for 50 paying families at ¥1,480. Sign an MOU with one community support center as the escalation partner. Log every alert and outcome so the pilot produces evidence for a municipal contract.

title: Pre-Procedure GLP-1 Readiness for Endoscopy and Ortho
one_liner: A 7-day workflow plus day-of gastric ultrasound that stops GLP-1 patients from being cancelled or aspirating at surgery centers.
customer: GI endoscopy centers, orthopedic groups, ASCs and their anesthesia groups.
problem: ASA reversed course in Oct 2024 and now advises most patients to continue GLP-1s, shifting the risk to residual gastric contents on the day. Centers cancel or abort cases, and 38% of GLP-1 users vs 8% of non-users were malnourished before joint surgery, which raises complication risk. There is no standard workflow, so every center improvises.
solution: Automated intake (drug, dose, indication, GI symptoms), tailored liquid-diet and hold instructions aligned to multi-society guidance, a malnutrition screen with a protein prehab plan, and nurse-performed gastric POCUS with AI-assisted antral grading and documentation on the day. Priced per case.
why_now: With ~22% of households containing a user, this is routine, not exceptional. Gastric POCUS studies are appearing (2025-26) and centers are looking for a defensible protocol after the 2024 guideline change.
revenue_model: $60-150 per GLP-1 patient case, plus anesthesia-group license and ultrasound rental.
non_obvious_insight: Centers will not stop scheduling GLP-1 patients, so the value is avoided same-day cancellations (thousands of dollars each) and defensible documentation. The buyer is the center's operations and anesthesia leadership, not the drug companies.
first_30_days: Sell to one endoscopy center and one anesthesia group. Supply paper-plus-SMS intake, protocols, a rented handheld ultrasound and training. Track cancellation rate before and after and price at $75 per case.

title: Peptide Assurance Mark for Clinics and Processors
one_liner: Independent lot testing and supplier audit with a QR-verifiable mark that lets peptide sellers pass payment-processor and insurer underwriting.
customer: 503A compounding pharmacies, peptide and longevity clinic chains, and the payment processors and insurers who need evidence to underwrite them.
problem: HHS moved ~14 of 19 Category 2 peptides (BPC-157, TB-500, GHK-Cu and others) back toward compoundable in Feb 2026, and an FDA panel backed BPC-157 and KPV on Jul 23. Clinics are multiplying, but Stripe and card networks exclude the category and Forbes (Jun 30, 2026) called it a '$1 billion industry banks won't touch'. Losing a merchant account kills sellers faster than FDA action.
solution: ISO 17025 lab partners test identity, purity, endotoxin, sterility and potency per lot. Supplier and chain-of-custody audits feed a public registry and QR verification that processors, insurers and state boards can accept, with annual certification and monitoring.
why_now: The legal window opened in 2026 with no infrastructure. Purity is uneven, and processors need third-party evidence to underwrite certified merchants.
revenue_model: $250-600 per lot test, $5-15k/year certification, and processor referral fees for certified merchants.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is payments and insurance, not FDA. A credible independent mark is the key that unlocks mainstream merchant accounts, so processors are the hidden buyer.
first_30_days: Contract an accredited lab and run a blind-purchase audit of 30 popular BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products, published as a report. Sell $500 audits to 10 clinics and approach two high-risk processors about fast-tracking certified merchants.

title: Launch and Reentry Airspace Forecasts for Airlines
one_liner: A dispatcher-facing forecast of whether launch and debris closures will really happen, and what rerouting will cost.
customer: Airline operations control centers on Caribbean, Atlantic and Pacific routes, cargo airlines, business-jet operators and flight-planning software vendors.
problem: Launches hit 321 in 2025, and Starship debris in early 2025 disrupted flights around Florida and the Caribbean. Launch slips and scrubs make late notices unreliable. Dispatchers over-buffer fuel and time or get surprised, and there is no probabilistic view of hazard areas.
solution: An API and dashboard that fuses launch manifests, vehicle-specific slip and scrub statistics, trajectory and debris-response-area models, and reentry predictions. It outputs closure probability and expected reroute cost per flight. Deliver it into existing flight-planning tools as a plug-in.
why_now: Cadence is climbing (223 launches in 2023 to 321 in 2025), Starship is flying orbital profiles, and new vehicles such as New Glenn and Stoke's Nova are coming. Airspace impact scales with cadence.
revenue_model: $30-150k per year per airline. Per-flight API fees through flight-planning vendors. Cargo and charter tiers.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable prediction is not where the hazard area is but whether the launch will actually go, which is a schedule-slip model. That converts publicly available manifests into a decision-quality product.
first_30_days: Backtest a slip and scrub model on the last 12 months of Florida and Vandenberg launches. Show it to five dispatch managers at airlines flying Caribbean routes. Offer a free pilot on one route and a paid tier for the next quarter.

title: Human Bench Network for AI Agents
one_liner: An API-fronted network of laid-off expert bench scientists who run ad hoc wet-lab experiments for AI agents and return machine-readable execution records.
customer: AI-first biotechs, AI-for-science startups and university groups (5-60 people, seed to Series B) that run agent swarms but have no wet lab; later, programs adjacent to frontier labs.
problem: Agent swarms now propose far more experiments than anyone can run. Anthropic's run went from 200,000+ reverse transcriptases to 20 candidates using ~950 agents in 21 hours. Stanford's Virtual Biotech (37,000 agents, Science, Sept 17, 2026) says the next step is testing findings in real labs. Cloud labs and robots handle fixed assays, but not ad hoc molecular biology: Anthropic itself found robotics less conducive to ad hoc workflows and kept human scientists at the bench. Human review and bench work are the bottleneck.
solution: Ticketed experiments through an API or MCP endpoint. The agent proposes a protocol and a senior scientist does feasibility triage. A vetted contractor then runs it at sublet or surplus benches, BSL-1/2 only. Each job returns a signed record that separates AI proposal, human edit and physical execution (deviations, photos, instrument logs, raw data). Fixed price per experiment. Start with commodity molecular biology: cloning, small-scale expression and purification, ELISA/BLI/qPCR, enzyme activity, bacterial and cell-culture assays.
why_now: Frontier labs and Stanford now say publicly that bench execution is the bottleneck. BioSpace tracks 15,000+ biopharma job cuts across 50+ companies in 2026, which supplies skilled hands. The OpenAI Foundation plans to distribute $1B by year-end through Public Data for Health, which creates grant-funded demand for data generation. Lab Manager notes there is no sign-off standard for AI-directed experiments, and this record format supplies one. Anthropic has said it wants to work with other scientists.
revenue_model: $1.5-8k per experiment at roughly 35-45% gross margin, monthly retainers with minimum volumes for agent-heavy customers, and a premium for 48-hour turnaround. The platform keeps a take rate on contractor labor.
non_obvious_insight: Compute is now nearly free compared with bench throughput, and robots failed as the universal answer because real biology is ad hoc. The defensible assets are a pre-vetted pool of humans and a structured execution record that agents can learn from. Humans become the last-mile actuator for AI. Adaptyv and cloud labs cover single fixed assays; nobody sells the long tail of one-off experiments.
first_30_days: Recruit 10-15 laid-off molecular biologists in Boston, SF and San Diego through layoff trackers and alumni groups. Rent 2-3 sublet benches or surplus CRO benches. Define three ticket types with fixed prices. Pitch 10 AI protein-design and agent startups and close 3-5 pilots. Aim for the first 20 paid experiments and publish the sample record schema.
